files.text:
Around 1650 Gaston d’Orléans, the king’s uncle, kept a botanical garden at Blois and paid a young engraver from Langres, Nicolas Robert, to paint its plants as they flowered: one plant to a sheet, life size where it would fit, in watercolour on vellum. When Gaston died the young Louis XIV took the sheets for himself and kept the painter on, and for nearly two centuries afterwards there was always someone at the Jardin du Roi in Paris whose work was to add to the king’s vellums. They are still there, almost seven thousand of them, in the library of the Muséum. Every collector of flowers who could afford it wanted the same thing for his own garden: a florilegium, a book of its rarest plants, painted on skin, to be turned over in the hand.

Pancrace Bessa was born in Paris in 1772 and learned the trade in the studio of Gerard van Spaendonck, the professor of flower painting at the Jardin, alongside Pierre-Joseph Redouté. He drew most of the plates for the Herbier général de l’amateur, and for the Duchesse de Berry he painted hundreds of flowers on vellum, for albums of her own. This one is a waratah from the sandstone country around Sydney, a plant few people in Paris had ever seen in flower.

Vellum is calfskin, soaked in lime until the hair slips, scraped, stretched on a frame and dried taut, then rubbed with pumice and chalk until it takes a brush. It is smooth, warm white and very slightly translucent, and nothing sinks into it. Paint stays on top, as bright as it went on, which is why patrons paid for it; and it stays soluble, which is what made it so hard to paint.

The drawing came first, in a hard, sharp graphite, light enough to disappear: the outline of the head, every floret in it, the edge of each leaf. Then the colour went on in thin transparent washes, one area at a time. On paper a wash soaks in and stays put. On vellum it stands on the skin as a pool, beads where it meets the dry surface, and dries with its pigment drawn to the rim; and a second wash brushed over it lifts the first. So the washes were kept few and pale, just the broad colour of the head, the bracts, the leaves and the stem.

The lights were not left as bare skin, as a watercolourist on paper would leave them. They were painted on top in body colour, pigment ground with lead white, which covers what is under it and dries pale and matte: the pink tips of the florets, the bloom on the leaves. Everything else was built with the point of a very small brush, nearly dry, in thousands of strokes laid side by side and across each other along the curve of every form, the way the miniature painters worked up a face. A stroke that small dries before it can disturb the paint beneath it. Done well, the hatching cannot be seen from a step away. There is only a flower.

What looks like one flower is a head of more than a hundred, packed on a cone and ringed by red bracts. Along the bottom of the sheet Bessa laid out a single one, taken apart for a botanist to read. The gold frame was ruled last, round all four sides, and the signature written under it in the same gold. The sheet is almost two hundred years old, and on vellum the red is as fierce as the day it dried.

# vellum-study Pancrace Bessa's waratah, a botanical watercolour on vellum from about 1830, painted in front of you as you scroll, in the order the Paris flower painters worked on calfskin. It starts as a sheet of bare vellum with a graphite underdrawing on it: the outline of the head, every floret, the edge of each leaf, and the frame ruled round the sheet. Then thin transparent washes go on, many small ones, leaves first and the red head last (one little pool per floret and bract). On vellum the water stands on the skin instead of sinking in, so each wash is a glossy pool with a hard, beaded edge that creeps across the drawing, and dries with its pigment pooled at the rim. The graphite shows through. Next come the lights in body colour, opaque touches of lead white and pigment laid over the wash (the pale tips of the florets, the bloom on the leaves), dab by dab. Each is darker and wet for a moment and dries pale and matte. Then the miniaturist's finish: strokes along the curve of each form appear all over it at once, stroke on stroke, broad ones first and hair-fine ones after, so each region comes into focus like a photograph: the leaves and stem first, then the bracts, and the head last and slowest, until the pooled washes have turned into a flower. Last, the gold frame is ruled round the sheet and the signature is written under it. The final frame is the painting, pixel for pixel. Scroll back and it un-paints. ```html
``` You can also `import { vellumStudy } from './vellum-study.js'` and call `vellumStudy(section, { src, mode, runway, webgl })`. It returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---------------|----------|-----------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The painting's JSON (size, vellum colour, stage windows, camera track). Beside it go `.webp` (the painting), `-bare.webp` (the vellum with no paint), `-wash.webp` (the first washes, dried), `-body.webp` (the washes with the body colour on them), `-model.webp` (the modelling the broad strokes lay in), `-lines.webp` (lossless, full size: R graphite, G body-colour opacity, B when the hair-fine strokes arrive) and `-map.webp` (lossless, half size: when the wash, the body-colour dabs, the broad strokes and the gold reach each point). | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned stage on a runway. `static`: the finished painting as an image. | | `data-runway` | `runway` | JSON, 380 | Section height in svh. The stage is pinned for `runway - 100` svh of travel. | | `data-webgl` | `webgl` | `on` | `off` leaves the finished painting as an image. | The stage windows (fractions of the runway, in the JSON's `stages`): washes 0.03-0.33, body colour 0.34-0.48, fine strokes 0.49-0.92 (the head alone takes 0.77-0.92), gold 0.93-0.97, then the finished sheet. The schedule is laid out in svh of travel offline: a big wash takes 12-18svh with two or three wet at once, and the head's strokes take about 43svh. Events (bubbling, so a sound can be wired to them later): `vellum-study:stage` with `detail: { stage }` as each layer begins while scrolling forward (`wash`, `body`, `hatch`, `gold`), and `vellum-study:done` when the signature is written. ## The real thing What we modelled, from the general record of how the *vélins du roi* and other florilegium vellums were painted, the miniature painters' practice of hatching and stippling, the Cleveland Museum of Art's record for this sheet (pencil and watercolour on parchment) and what the scan itself shows at full size: graphite contours still visible at the petal edges, transparent washes, opaque pale touches over them, and fine strokes everywhere. We found no technical study of this sheet. The watercolour transients follow Curtis et al., *Computer-Generated Watercolor*, SIGGRAPH 1997: - **The skin.** Vellum is calfskin limed, scraped, stretched and pounced with pumice and chalk. It does not absorb. Paint dries on top of it, stays brilliant and stays soluble: a wet brush over a dry wash lifts it. - **Graphite first.** A hard, light pencil outline of every form, here grey and slightly cool, catching on the grain. It stays visible through the transparent washes, disappears under body colour, and is worked over by the strokes. - **Washes that stand on the surface.** A thin transparent wash per small area: each floret and bract of the head is its own little pool, a leaf is one, laid in the order of a sweep through the object. The wet front advances unevenly with a hard meniscus at its edge (the bead, darker), the standing water is darker and glossy, and as it dries, edges first and the middle last in islands, the pigment is drawn to the rim. A dried wash pools: darker toward the lower and outer edge of its area, lighter where the brush lifted, with a fine dark tide line at its rim and, in a few places, a cauliflower bloom (a pale lobe with a dark frilled edge). Because a second wash would lift the first, there is one. - **Body colour for the lights.** Pigment with lead white, opaque. It is laid in touches, dab by dab (short elongated strokes along the form), over the dry wash: the pale tips of the florets, the lights of the bracts, the bloom on the leaves. Wet gouache is darker and more saturated and dries paler and matte. - **The miniaturist's finish.** All the modelling is built with the tip of a small brush, nearly dry, in strokes laid along the form, all over the form at once and stroke on stroke: broader strokes lay in the modelling, finer ones sharpen it, so the whole region comes into focus together, region by region. Each stroke is a shade darker for an instant while wet. This is where the colour gets its depth and the flower its roundness, so it is the slowest pass. - **Gold and signature last.** The frame is ruled in gold round the four sides, then the signature written under it. Simplified: time is compressed into scroll. One first wash per area, where a painter might lay two or three very thin ones. Strokes are revealed from the finished painting along a flow field taken from its own brushwork (see below), so they lie where Bessa's strokes do, but they are not his strokes one for one, nor in his order. The order of objects is a plausible working order, not documented for this sheet. The gold is laid as one pass, without the mordant and burnishing. ## How it works **Offline (Python, scripts kept in the builder's scratch folder, not in the component).** All in linear-light optical density, `D = -ln(colour / vellum)`. 1. *Masks and objects.* The paint is separated from the vellum by density and chroma, and the gold frame and signature by hue inside a band. The plant is split by colour (red, green, other) and then into fourteen objects (head, two groups of bracts, seven leaves, stem, three dissections) by a marker watershed on the colour gradient, each colour group on its own, with stray islands folded into the object round them (or, for a red piece cut off by a leaf lying over it, into the nearest red object). 2. *Bare vellum.* Under the paint, the vellum is filled from the bare skin around it (normalised convolution at three scales) plus the skin's real texture (a mirrored tile of the scan's high frequencies). The faint halo the scan has for about 25px round the paint is taken out, and comes back when the paint next to it is finished. 3. *Flat.* The hatching is removed (median, then bilateral twice) and the forms kept. It is used to place the washes, the body colour and the pencil. 4. *First wash.* The head, bracts and dissections are cut into small areas that follow the painting's own forms (a watershed of the flat image's gradient from its h-minima: each floret tip, each dark gap, each bract); a leaf or the stem is one area (split only where a different colour lies in it). Each area's tone is half its median and half the flat colour diffused inside that area only (a barrier at every border, so nothing blurs across an edge), at about 56% of the density. Then it pools: x(0.84 + 0.22·depth down the area + 0.24·nearness to its rim + fBm), a 0.85px dark tide line at every border, and a frilly cauliflower bloom in about one area in eleven. 5. *Body colour.* Where the flat image is lighter than its neighbourhood (a median over ~70px) and lighter than the wash beneath, it can only be opaque paint on top. The wash under each touch is carried on from the wash around it (the floret was washed whole), the touch is given a crisp 1px edge, and it is split into dabs: ellipses 12-20px long and 4-7px wide along the brushwork's direction, ordered down the touch. 6. *Graphite.* Canny edges of the flat image at half size, plus the object outlines, skeletonised, pruned, and drawn as a soft line about 2.5px wide (full size) whose pressure wanders. The frame is ruled as four straight lines. 7. *Time maps.* The wash arrives along a geodesic sweep through each object (scikit-image `MCP_Geometric` over a noisy speed field) from its start. Body touches go in the order of that sweep, each brushed from its upper end. The fine strokes: a structure tensor of the painting's own luminance gives the direction of the brushwork. White noise is integrated along it (line-integral Two sets of strokes are traced along it from jittered seeds and kept inside their object: broad ones (half size, ~20px long, 3px wide) and hair-fine ones (full size, ~22px long, 3px wide, 240,000 of them). Each stroke gets its own random moment: 0.2 x the object's sweep + 0.8 x a random draw (broad strokes in the first 72% of the object's window, fine ones from 18% on), drawn so that the earliest stroke over any pixel is uniformly spread. A pixel's time is that of the earliest stroke over it, softened by ~0.8px. Pixels off the plant take the time of the nearest paint (their pencil goes with it). The gold runs clockwise round the frame, then the signature left to right. A camera track (the centroid of whatever is active) goes in the JSON. **In the browser.** One quad, one fragment shader (WebGL2, or WebGL1 without the mip blur and the phone zoom). Per pixel, in density, the layers nest: `D = mix(mix(mix(mix(D_bare, W', cw), B', cb), D_M, cl), D_O, max(cf, cg))`, where `cw`, `cb`, `cl`, `cf` and `cg` are the wash, body-colour, broad-stroke, fine-stroke and gold coverage from the time maps, `D_M` is the body-colour stage plus the painting's modelling softened by 3.5px, and the primes are the wet looks (wash: blurred by a mip bias, darker, a beaded front, a transient rim as it dries, islands; body colour: darker until it dries, then a hair proud of the skin, lit on its upper left edge; strokes: a shade darker for an instant). The colour is `O · exp(-(D - D_O))`. When every layer is down and dry this is exactly `O`, the painting. The graphite is multiplied on top and goes as the paint covers it. - Images are resampled on the CPU to the size they are shown at, then mipmapped. The time map and the lines are uploaded exact (unpremultiplied ImageBitmaps) and sampled linearly (the lines mipmapped). - Scroll is followed on a critically damped spring (quicker going back). - The canvas draws the sheet itself: its edge sharp and anti-aliased, wandering by a hair, with a tight shadow that lifts a little in places where the skin cockles. No vignette. The scan is cropped inside the sheet, so the edge is drawn, not the original's. - On a narrow screen (under 760px) the sheet fills the width. From the first wash the view goes a little closer (up to 1.4x), and for the fine strokes about 2.15x, following the active region. It pulls back to the whole sheet before the gold. The camera is a function of scroll only. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---------------|-----------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the page around the sheet (read from the section's background) | | `--vs-gutter` | `var(--gutter)` | side padding of the stage (the demo uses 6px on phones so the sheet fills the width) | | `--vs-runway` | set by the script | section height in scroll mode | The sheet keeps the vellum's own colour, a cool white a shade off the page. ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS, without WebGL, or with `data-webgl="off"`, the finished painting is an ``. The canvas is `aria-hidden`. The art is ornament (`alt=""`), and the credits are in `assets/credits.json`. - Reduced motion: no runway and no canvas, only the finished painting. If the setting changes mid-visit, it settles on the finished painting. - Phone: nothing is interactive, so a swipe always scrolls (tested on the pinned stage). - There is no UI and no caption. The piece is driven by scroll alone. ## Cost - Assets 3.2 MB: lines 1.6 MB (lossless: graphite, body opacity and the fine strokes' times), painting 0.59 MB, time map 0.37 MB (lossless, half size), model 0.22 MB, body 0.19 MB, wash 0.17 MB, bare 0.05 MB, JSON 12 KB. - One full-screen quad, about fifteen texture reads per pixel. A frame draws only while the scroll spring is moving and the section is on screen (IntersectionObserver). Nothing runs when the scroll is still, off screen or in a hidden tab. DPR is capped at 2. ## Making another painting The scripts (`s1_mask.py` paint, gold and vellum colour; `s2_classes.py` colour groups; `s3_objects.py` objects from marker lines; `s4_layers.py` bare vellum, flat, the small pooled washes; `s5_body.py` body colour and its dabs; `s6_times.py` graphite, time maps, schedule, camera and export) live in the builder's scratch folder. A new sheet needs its own marker lines per object, the gold band, and a plain patch of vellum for the texture tile. Look at the bare vellum (contrast-stretched), the first wash and the body colour at full size before exporting. The mistakes show there: ghosts of the plant in the bare skin, blotchy tones, touches on the wrong object. ## Credits Pancrace Bessa, untitled study of a waratah (*Telopea speciosissima*), 1828–1835, pencil and watercolour on vellum. The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland in honor of Mrs. William G. Mather, 1955.484. Open Access, CC0.
